name: Natural Rights
statement: Some rights belong to people by their very nature, universal and inalienable, prior to any government.
meaning: Natural rights are rights held to be inherent in human beings by virtue of their nature, or granted by God or nature, and therefore universal, inalienable, and existing independently of any particular government or legal system. They are contrasted with legal or positive rights, which are conferred by a particular society or state and vary across cultures and governments. The idea has roots in ancient and medieval natural law, in the thought of Aristotle, the Stoics, Cicero, and Thomas Aquinas, and it was developed in the early modern period by thinkers including Hugo Grotius and Thomas Hobbes, who spoke of a natural right to self-preservation. The most influential account is John Locke's, who held that individuals in the state of nature possess natural rights to life, liberty, and property, which government exists to protect. Natural rights theory profoundly shaped the great documents of the age of revolution: the American Declaration of Independence of 1776 proclaimed that people are endowed with unalienable rights including life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, and the French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789 asserted natural rights. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries the language of natural rights largely gave way to that of human rights, but the underlying idea remains foundational to modern rights discourse.
mechanism: Natural rights theory grounds certain rights in human nature rather than in the will of any lawgiver, and this grounding gives the rights their distinctive properties. The reasoning typically holds that because human beings have a certain nature, as rational, free, or created beings, they possess entitlements that any legitimate authority must respect, entitlements that they have simply as humans and not because any state has granted them. From this follow the characteristic features of natural rights: they are universal, belonging to all people everywhere; inalienable, meaning a person cannot lose them through bad conduct or even voluntarily give them up; and imprescriptible, not extinguished by the passage of time or by law. Natural rights are usually understood within the broader framework of natural law, the idea of a moral order discoverable by reason that stands above human legislation; natural rights are the entitlements that this moral order confers on individuals. In Locke's influential version, people in the state of nature already hold rights to life, liberty, and property under natural law, and they form government precisely to secure these pre-existing rights, so that a government which violates them betrays its purpose and may lose its legitimacy. Because they are prior to and independent of the state, natural rights serve as a standard against which laws and governments can be judged and, if necessary, resisted.

examples.text: John Locke held that people possess natural rights to life, liberty, and property, which government exists to protect.
The American Declaration of 1776 proclaimed unalienable rights including life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
Natural rights are held to exist independently of any state, as a standard against which laws can be judged.

variants.name: Natural law versus natural rights
variants.text: Natural law is the broader moral order discoverable by reason, while natural rights are the entitlements it confers on individuals.

variants.name: The turn to human rights
variants.text: The later shift from the language of natural rights to that of human rights, especially after the Second World War.

whyItMatters: Natural rights are among the most consequential ideas in the history of political thought, providing the intellectual foundation for the modern conception of human rights and for limits on the power of the state. By holding that individuals possess rights simply by virtue of being human, rights that no government grants and none may rightfully violate, natural rights theory gave people a powerful standard for judging laws and rulers and a justification for resisting tyranny. This idea animated the great revolutions and founding documents of the modern age, from the American Declaration of Independence, which drew on Locke to proclaim unalienable rights, to the French Declaration of the Rights of Man, and it flowed into the twentieth-century framework of human rights enshrined in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The concepts of universal, inalienable rights prior to the state continue to underpin constitutional government, the rule of law, and appeals to justice against oppression. Even as philosophers debate how such rights can be grounded, the language of natural and human rights remains central to moral and political argument worldwide.

working.text: hold that human beings possess certain entitlements simply by virtue of their nature, not by grant of any state.
conclude that such rights are universal, inalienable, and prior to and independent of any government.
use natural rights as a standard against which laws and governments can be measured and, if they violate them, resisted.

limits: Natural rights are foundational but have long been philosophically contested, above all over how they can be grounded. Legal positivists and utilitarians reject the idea that rights exist independently of the state, arguing that rights are creations of law; Jeremy Bentham famously dismissed natural rights as simple nonsense and natural and imprescriptible rights as nonsense upon stilts, holding that only the state can confer rights. Critics also point to the difficulty of justifying which rights are natural and why, since different thinkers have proposed different lists, and to cultural-relativist objections that the notion reflects a particular Western tradition rather than a universal truth. The very properties claimed for natural rights, universality and inalienability, are asserted rather than easily demonstrated. Partly for these reasons, the language of natural rights largely gave way to that of human rights, which are often defended on other grounds.
misreadings: Natural rights are not the same as legal rights granted by a particular government; they are claimed to exist independently of any state, which is precisely what critics like Bentham dispute. Their existence is not a settled fact but a contested philosophical position, since positivists and utilitarians deny that rights precede the law. And the list of which rights are natural is not fixed or self-evident, varying among thinkers, so treating natural rights as identical to legal rights, as beyond dispute, or as an agreed and obvious list, misreads a powerful but philosophically contested doctrine.
origin: The idea, rooted in ancient and medieval natural law and developed by Grotius, Hobbes, and especially Locke, that human beings possess universal, inalienable rights by their nature, prior to and independent of any government.
